summary: This proposed standard specifies a DNS resource record for use with the Host Identity Protocol. The record lets a HIP node store in DNS its Host Identity, the public part of its key pair, and its Host Identity Tag, a hash of that key, along with rendezvous server info.

plainLanguage.summary:
With the Host Identity Protocol, a host proves who it is with a public key instead of an IP address. That leaves a gap in the DNS: there was no record type for publishing a public key.

This RFC adds one. A HIP record holds the public key, a short hash of it called the tag, and optionally the name of a rendezvous server that can forward the first handshake packet to the host. A host that moves can then keep one name in the DNS and let the rendezvous server keep track of where it actually is.

subtitle: A DNS record type that publishes a HIP host's public key, its tag and its rendezvous servers.

tldr.problem: A host that uses the Host Identity Protocol is identified by a public key rather than by its IP address, but the DNS only knows how to publish IP addresses. So a peer that has a name has no way to learn the public key it needs before starting a HIP exchange.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a DNS resource record of type HIP that carries the public key algorithm, the Host Identity, the Host Identity Tag and, optionally, the domain names of the host's rendezvous servers. It also defines the wire format, the zone-file format and how a host uses the record to start a connection.
tldr.outcome: A host can be found by name and reached through a rendezvous server even when its IP address keeps changing. The RFC obsoletes RFC 5205 and adds support for elliptic-curve keys.

today: RFC 8005 is a Proposed Standard from October 2016. It obsoletes RFC 5205 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The HIP record type is registered as type 55 in the IANA DNS resource record type registry, and the ECDSA key algorithm value as 3 in the IPSECKEY algorithm type registry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document specifies a resource record for the Domain Name System and how to use it with the Host Identity Protocol. The record allows a HIP node to store in the DNS its Host Identity, the public component of the node's public-private key pair, its Host Identity Tag, a truncated hash of that key, and the domain names of its rendezvous servers.

Most Internet applications that need to communicate with a remote host first translate a domain name into one or more IP addresses, before any communication takes place, and this step relies on a DNS lookup.

With HIP, IP addresses are intended to be used mostly for on-the-wire communication between end hosts, while most upper layer protocols and applications use Host Identities or Host Identity Tags instead. Consequently, a means is needed to translate a domain name into a Host Identity. Using the DNS for this translation is straightforward: upon a query for a name-to-IP-address lookup, the resolver would additionally perform a name-to-Host-Identity lookup and use it to construct the resulting Host-Identity-to-IP-address mapping, which is internal to the HIP layer.

The HIP specification defines the HIP base exchange between an Initiator and a Responder based on a four-way handshake involving four HIP packets, I1, R1, I2 and R2. Since the HIP packets contain both the Initiator and the Responder Host Identity Tag, the Initiator needs to know the Responder's Host Identity and Tag before initiating the base exchange by sending an I1 packet. The HIP Rendezvous Extension allows a HIP node to be reached via the IP addresses of a third party, its rendezvous server, so a means is also needed to find the name of a rendezvous server for a given host name.
sections.plainLanguage: The point is to close the gap between the DNS and HIP. The DNS knows names and addresses; HIP needs names to turn into public keys.

sections.title: Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
With HIP, most applications and upper layer protocols are unaware of the IP addresses used to carry packets on the wire. Consequently, a HIP node could take advantage of having multiple IP addresses for failover, redundancy, mobility or renumbering, in a manner transparent to most applications, because they are bound to Host Identities.

For a node to be reachable by reference to its Fully Qualified Domain Name, the DNS should hold a set of IP addresses through A and AAAA resource record sets, and a Host Identity, a Host Identity Tag and possibly a set of rendezvous servers through HIP records. The HIP record is class independent.

When a HIP node wants to initiate communication with another HIP node, it first needs to perform a HIP base exchange to set up an association towards its peer. Although such an exchange can be initiated opportunistically, that is, without prior knowledge of the Responder's Host Identity, by doing so both nodes knowingly risk man-in-the-middle attacks. To prevent these attacks, it is recommended that the Initiator first obtains the Host Identity of the Responder, which can be done through manual configuration or DNS lookups.

When a HIP node is frequently changing its IP addresses, the natural DNS latency for propagating changes may prevent it from publishing its new addresses in the DNS. The HIP Architecture introduces rendezvous servers for this problem: a HIP host uses a rendezvous server as a rendezvous point to maintain reachability with possible HIP Initiators while moving. Such a node would publish in the DNS its rendezvous server domain names in a HIP record, while keeping its rendezvous servers up-to-date with its current set of IP addresses.

A static, single-homed host stores its Host Identity and Host Identity Tag in a HIP record at its own name, and an Initiator queries for the HIP record and then for the A and AAAA records. A mobile host stores its Host Identity, its tag and the name or names of its rendezvous servers, and the Initiator queries for the HIP record at the host name and then for the A and AAAA records of the rendezvous server name.
sections.plainLanguage: Two situations are described. A fixed host simply publishes its key under its own name. A host that moves publishes its key under its own name too, but adds the name of a relay server, and the Initiator sends the first packet to the relay rather than to the host.

sections.title: Using the DNS with HIP
sections.content:
For any HIP node, its Host Identity, the associated Host Identity Tag and the fully qualified domain name of its possible rendezvous servers can be stored in a DNS HIP record. Upon return of a HIP record, a host must always calculate the Host-Identity-derivative Host Identity Tag to be used in the HIP exchange, while the tag included in the record should only be used as an optimization, for example a table lookup.

The HIP record may also contain one or more domain names of rendezvous servers towards which HIP I1 packets might be sent to trigger the establishment of an association with the entity named by the record. The Rendezvous Server field of a record stored at a given owner name may include the owner name itself, and a semantically equivalent situation occurs if no rendezvous server is present in the record stored at that owner name. Such situations occur in two cases: the host is mobile and the A or AAAA records stored at its host name contain the addresses of its rendezvous server rather than its own, or the host is stationary and can be reached directly at the addresses in those records, which is a degenerate case where the host acts as a rendezvous server for itself.

On a HIP node, a HIP exchange should be initiated whenever an upper layer protocol attempts to communicate with an entity and the DNS lookup returns HIP records. HIP records have a Time To Live associated with them: when the number of seconds that passed since the record was retrieved exceeds the record's TTL, the record must be considered no longer valid and deleted by the entity that retrieved it, and a new query must be made to retrieve a fresh copy.

There may be multiple HIP records associated with a single name. It is outside the scope of this specification how a host chooses between them. The rendezvous server information may be copied and aligned across multiple records, or may be different for each one; a host must check that the rendezvous server used is associated with the Host Identity being used, when multiple choices are present.
sections.plainLanguage: The record holds a hint that the host should check for itself rather than trust, and it goes stale on the same schedule as any other DNS record.

sections.title: The HIP Record Storage Format
sections.content:
The data of a HIP record consists of a public key algorithm type, the HIT length, a HIT, a public key, that is, a Host Identity, and optionally one or more rendezvous servers. The HIT length, public key algorithm, public key length, HIT and public key fields are required; the Rendezvous Server field is optional.

The HIT length indicates the length in bytes of the HIT field and is an 8-bit unsigned integer. The public key algorithm field indicates the public key cryptographic algorithm and the implied public key field format, and is also an 8-bit unsigned integer; the document reuses the values defined for the algorithm type of the IPSECKEY resource record.

The public key length indicates the length in bytes of the public key field and is a 16-bit unsigned integer in network byte order. The HIT is stored as a binary value in network byte order.

Two of the public key types, RSA and DSA, reuse the key formats defined for the IPSECKEY resource record. The DSA key format is defined in RFC 2536 and the RSA key format in RFC 3110, with the RSA key size limit of 4096 bits relaxed in the IPSECKEY specification. The document also defines the key format of type Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm as the algorithm-specific portion of the DNSKEY record data for ECDSA, that is, all of the record data after the first four octets.

The Rendezvous Server field indicates one or more variable-length wire-encoded domain names of rendezvous servers, concatenated and encoded as described in the DNS implementation specification, where a domain name is a series of labels terminated by a label of zero length. Since the wire-encoded format is self-describing, the length of each domain name is implicit, and the zero-length label termination serves as a separator between multiple names concatenated in the same record. The domain names must not be compressed, and the rendezvous servers are listed in order of preference, which defines an implicit order among the servers of a single record. When multiple HIP records are present at the same owner name, this implicit order must not be used to infer a preference order between servers stored in different records.
sections.plainLanguage: The record is a small fixed header followed by two variable-length blobs, the tag and the key, and then the optional list of relay server names. The header says how long each blob is, so the record can be parsed without any extra information.

sections.title: The Zone File Presentation Format
sections.content:
The representation of the HIP record in a zone master file omits the HIT length field, since it is implicitly known from the HIT field representation, and omits the public key length field, since it is implicitly known from the public key representation containing no whitespace.

The public key algorithm field is represented as an unsigned integer. The HIT field is represented as the Base16 encoding, that is, hexadecimal, of the HIT, and the encoding must not contain whitespace, to distinguish it from the public key field. The public key field is represented as the Base64 encoding of the key, and the encoding must not contain whitespace, to distinguish it from the rendezvous server field. The rendezvous server field is represented by one or more domain names separated by whitespace, which is only used in the presentation format and is not part of the wire format.
sections.plainLanguage: In a zone file the record looks like a small parenthesised list: a number, then the tag in hex, then the key in base64, then any server names. The whitespace between them is what separates one field from the next.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: The RFC gives three examples of a HIP record in a zone file. The first is a node with a Host Identity and a Host Identity Tag but no rendezvous server. The second is a node with a Host Identity, a Host Identity Tag and one rendezvous server. The third is a node with a Host Identity, a Host Identity Tag and two rendezvous servers. In each case the algorithm field holds the value 2, and the tag is given in hexadecimal while the key is given in base64 and wrapped across lines because it does not fit on one.
sections.plainLanguage: The three examples are the same record with nothing, one and two relay server names added, so the optional field is easy to see.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The HIP DNS extension allows two HIP nodes to be provisioned with the public keying material of their peer, which is then used in a key exchange between them. It is therefore subject, in the same way as the IPSECKEY record, to threats stemming from attacks against unsecured HIP records.

A HIP node should obtain HIP records from a trusted party through a secure channel ensuring data integrity and authenticity of the records. DNSSEC provides such a secure channel, but it only offers data integrity and authenticity guarantees to the channel between the DNS server publishing a zone and the HIP node; it does not ensure that the entity publishing the zone is trusted. The signature of the HIP record set must therefore not be misinterpreted as a certificate binding the Host Identity or the Host Identity Tag to the owner name.

An attacker able to tamper with an unsecured HIP record can mount man-in-the-middle attacks on the cryptographic core of the eventual HIP exchange, because the record holds the peer's public key and its hash. Such an attacker can also redirect I1 packets sent to the named peer, because the record may hold a rendezvous server domain name that is resolved into a destination address. The two attacks can be used in conjunction, replacing the Responder's Host Identity and the rendezvous server address in a spoofed DNS packet and then redirecting all exchanged packets. In that case HIP provides neither confidentiality nor Initiator Host Identity protection from eavesdroppers.

Because some secure hashes eventually become insecure, as the SHA-1 hash used by HIP to generate a HIT from a Host Identity is expected to, a HIP end-node implementation should not authenticate its HIP peers based solely on a HIT retrieved from the DNS, but should use Host-Identity-based authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: The record holds a public key, so anyone who can rewrite it in the DNS can impersonate the host. DNSSEC protects the record in transit, but it does not vouch for the zone itself, and the short tag must not be trusted on its own.

messages.label: HIP? www.example.com
messages.note: The initiator asks for the HIP record at the host name.

messages.label: HIT-R, HI-R, rvs.example.com
messages.note: The answer holds the host's tag, its public key and the name of its rendezvous server.

messages.label: A? rvs.example.com
messages.note: The initiator then asks for the address of the rendezvous server.

messages.label: A IP-RVS
messages.note: The answer holds the rendezvous server's address.

messages.label: I1
messages.note: The initiator sends the first HIP packet to the rendezvous server rather than to the host.

messages.label: I1
messages.note: The rendezvous server relays the packet to the host's current address, which completes the exchange.

items.title: HIT
items.text: Written as Base16, that is, hexadecimal, with no whitespace.

items.text: Written as Base64 with no whitespace, which is what tells the parser where the key ends.

items.title: Rendezvous Servers
items.text: Written as one or more domain names separated by whitespace.
